title: Monitoring vs Observability for Data Pipelines

scenes.heading: Monitoring vs Observability
scenes.narration: Monitoring and observability sound similar, but they answer fundamentally different kinds of questions about your pipelines.

scenes.heading: The core difference
scenes.narration: Monitoring tracks the failures you already anticipated, telling you when a known metric crosses a threshold. Observability lets you ask new questions you never predefined, so you can dig into why something broke. Monitoring tells you the pipeline is late; observability helps you discover it was a single skewed partition.

scenes.heading: Signals that matter for data
bullets: Volume: row counts drifting up or down
Freshness: how current the data is
Schema: unexpected columns or type changes
Distribution: values shifting away from normal
Lineage: which downstream tables are affected
scenes.narration: Row volume reveals dropped or duplicated loads. Freshness shows whether data is arriving on time. Schema signals catch unexpected structural changes. Distribution checks surface subtle corruption where counts look fine but values are wrong. And lineage ties any failure to the downstream tables and dashboards it touches.

scenes.heading: From alert to answer
scenes.narration: A monitor fires the first alert that something is wrong. Then observability tooling lets you trace the data's path and pinpoint the exact failing stage. Finally, lineage confirms the blast radius so you know who to notify and what to backfill.

scenes.text: Monitoring catches the failures you predicted; observability helps you understand the ones you didn't. Mature teams invest in both.
scenes.narration: Monitoring catches the failures you predicted, while observability helps you understand the ones you never saw coming, and mature data teams deliberately invest in both.
